title: Customer Interview Guide (Case Studies + Reference Program)
author: Ethan Wallace
content:
## Purpose
This guide provides a repeatable interview script and question bank for producing:
1) Public case studies (web + PDF) and/or
2) Reference call profiles (internal-only)

It is designed to capture credible, measurable production outcomes (latency, cost, reliability), plus architectural and deployment details across **Hosted**, **Dedicated**, and **Private** deployments—without collecting sensitive information that will block legal/security approvals.

## Audience
- **Interviewers:** Marketing (writer/PMM), Solutions Engineering, Customer Success
- **Interviewees:** Customer engineering + business stakeholders

Typical interviewees by persona:
- Engineering: platform lead, ML engineer, infra/SRE, security/compliance
- Business: product owner, VP Eng, head of support/ops, procurement sponsor

## When to use this guide
Use for any customer moving into:
- Public case study track (logo/quote/metrics publishing)
- Reference-call track (internal profile + scheduled calls)
- “Anonymized case study” track (no logo, limited industry + details)

## Pre-interview checklist (do this 48–72 hours before)
**Owner:** Interviewer (Marketing) with AE/CSM support

1) **Confirm track and constraints**
   - Public vs internal-only
   - Allowed level of detail (architecture diagram? regions? model names?)
   - Whether metrics may be published (and in what form)

2) **Confirm attendees and roles**
   - Customer spokesperson (name/title)
   - Technical validator (who can confirm numbers and architecture)
   - Legal/Comms approver (who signs releases)

3) **Send pre-read (email)**
   - Interview agenda + timebox
   - Metrics worksheet (ask them to bring baseline/current numbers)
   - Draft “safe list” of topics and “do-not-share” topics

4) **Set up recording + notes**
   - Ask permission to record (required)
   - Decide note-taker
   - Store recording in approved system (per CS/Legal guidelines)

5) **Align internally on narrative angle**
   - Which Redwood differentiator(s) this story should prove:
     - Latency/throughput
     - Unit cost (cost per token / cost per query)
     - Reliability and fallback/graceful degradation
     - Deployment flexibility (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
     - Operational visibility (Console, tracing, rollouts)

## Interview formats (recommended)
### Option A: Single 60-minute combined interview (fast path)
- 10 min: Business context + decision process
- 35 min: Technical deep dive + metrics
- 10 min: Outcomes + quotes
- 5 min: Next steps + approvals

### Option B: Two-part interview (best for enterprise / Private)
1) 45–60 min technical interview (engineering + security)
2) 30–45 min business interview (product/ops leader)

## Standard opening script (read verbatim)
“Thanks for making time. The goal today is to capture the story of what you built, why you chose Redwood Inference, and what changed in production—especially measurable outcomes like latency, reliability, and cost. We’ll ask some technical questions so we can be accurate.

Before we start: are you comfortable if we record this call for internal drafting purposes? The recording will not be shared externally. For anything public, we’ll send you a draft and nothing will be published without your written approval.”

If public case study track:
“Separately, we’ll propose a small set of metrics and quotes for publication. You will have full control over what’s included and we can keep sensitive details out.”

## Ground rules (say out loud)
- “If anything feels sensitive, please stop us and we’ll reframe.”
- “We’ll avoid customer PII, internal hostnames, security architecture details that increase risk, and any undisclosed vendor relationships.”
- “We’ll validate all numbers (source + window) before publishing.”

## Question bank (core)
Use what’s relevant. Do not try to ask everything.

### 1) Customer and use case (5–10 min)
1. What product/workflow uses LLM inference today?
2. Who are the end users (internal agents, customers, developers)?
3. What are the key user journeys?
   - Examples: support reply drafting, RAG search + rerank, code assistant, summarization, classification
4. What does “good” look like for the end user (speed, quality, uptime)?
5. What are the top constraints?
   - Regulated data, data residency, PII/PHI, audit logging, latency SLOs, cost ceilings

### 2) Prior state and why change (baseline) (10 min)
1. What was your previous inference approach?
   - Another API provider, self-hosted vLLM/TGI, cloud GPU endpoints, hybrid
2. What was working well? What was not?
3. What triggered the search for a new solution?
   - Latency spikes, unpredictable cost, GPU ops burden, security posture, reliability incidents
4. What alternatives did you evaluate?
5. What were the decision criteria and “must-haves”?

### 3) Success criteria (get measurable) (5–10 min)
Capture both **targets** and **non-negotiables**.
1. Latency targets (p50/p95) and how you measure them
2. Throughput targets (RPS, tokens/sec, concurrency)
3. Reliability targets
   - error rate, timeouts, availability, incident frequency
4. Cost targets
   - cost per 1k tokens, cost per request, monthly budget, margin constraints
5. Security/compliance targets
   - SOC 2, audit logs, KMS/HSM, retention, VPC/on-prem

### 4) Deployment model rationale (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) (10–15 min)
Ask this even if they “already chose”—it creates a clean narrative.

**Hosted API**
- What made Hosted viable for your workload?
- What guardrails did you need (rate limits, quotas, regional routing)?
- Any concerns about multi-tenancy and how were they addressed?

**Dedicated capacity**
- What required predictable throughput/latency enough to reserve capacity?
- What does your traffic pattern look like (bursty vs steady; time-of-day peaks)?
- How did you evaluate autoscaling/burst behavior?
- What isolation requirements mattered (data isolation, noisy neighbor avoidance)?

**Private (VPC / on-prem)**
- What specific requirements drove Private?
  - customer-managed networking, private control plane, inbound/outbound restrictions
- Key management: do you require customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM)? Who owns key rotation?
- Audit logging: what fields and retention requirements do you have?
- Any penetration testing, vendor risk, or procurement milestones that impacted timeline?

### 5) Architecture and implementation (15–25 min)
Goal: enough detail to be credible, not enough to create security risk.

1. High-level system diagram (talk it through)
   - Where does Redwood sit in the request path?
   - What upstream services call Redwood?
   - What is downstream (post-processing, storage, analytics)?

2. Models and routes
   - Which capabilities are used (chat/text generation, embeddings, reranking)?
   - Do you use multiple models for different routes?
   - Are model versions pinned? Any rollout/canary policies?

3. Prompting and output requirements
   - Structured output / JSON schema needs
   - Tool/function calling
   - Streaming requirements (SSE/websocket patterns, token streaming)

4. Performance and cost controls
   - Batching: do you batch requests? Any workload-aware batching?
   - Caching: prefix/KV cache; prompt caching; “same doc” reuse patterns
   - Quantization profiles: did you adopt quantization? How did you validate quality?
   - Routing: cost/latency policies; regional routing; fallbacks

5. Observability and operations
   - What do you monitor (latency percentiles, token usage, error types, queue depth)?
   - How do you debug (Console dashboards, tracing hooks, logs)?
   - Alerting and on-call: who gets paged and for what thresholds?

6. Rollout timeline
   - First integration date → first production traffic → full rollout
   - Biggest implementation risk and how you mitigated it

### 6) Reliability and incident history (high-signal section) (10–15 min)
We are not looking for “perfect.” We are looking for clear handling and improvements.

1. What failure modes mattered most?
   - timeouts, 429s/rate limits, capacity constraints, model regressions, streaming disconnects
2. Any incidents in the last 3–6 months related to inference?
   - What happened, impact, how detected, how mitigated
3. What safeguards did you implement?
   - fallbacks to compatible model variants
   - retry/backoff strategies
   - circuit breakers
   - staged rollouts/canaries
4. What is the current operational posture?
   - SLOs/SLA expectations, incident runbooks, escalation paths

### 7) Outcomes and proof points (must be attributable) (10–15 min)
Ask for **before/after** and **measurement notes**.

1. What changed after adopting Redwood?
   - Latency (p50/p95), throughput, error rate, stability
   - Cost per token / cost per query / monthly spend
   - Engineering time saved (GPU ops reduction, fewer incident hours)

2. What is the measurement window?
   - e.g., “30-day trailing window,” “peak weekday hours,” “A/B test over N requests”

3. What is the baseline comparison?
   - previous provider, self-hosted stack, older model/version, or earlier infra

4. Can you share supporting evidence?
   - dashboards, exported metrics, anonymized screenshots

5. What caveats should we include to be honest?
   - workload specifics, context, traffic shape, prompt length, region

### 8) Quotes and positioning (5–10 min)
Goal: 2–4 quotable lines from both technical and business angles.

Prompts:
- “What were you most skeptical about before choosing Redwood?”
- “What surprised you most after going live?”
- “If you recommended Redwood to a peer, what would you say?”
- “What does Redwood let your team do that you couldn’t do before?”

If they struggle, offer templates to react to:
- “Redwood helped us hit predictable p95 latency without over-provisioning GPUs.”
- “We reduced cost per query while keeping output quality stable.”
- “Private deployment + audit logging unblocked our compliance timeline.”
- “Fallback policies and rollouts reduced risk of model changes.”

### 9) Reference participation logistics (only if applicable) (5 min)
1. Are you open to reference calls? Under what conditions?
2. Preferred cadence (e.g., 1–2 per quarter) and scheduling windows
3. Topics you’re happy to discuss vs off-limits
4. Who should be the default reference(s)? Backup contact?

## Metrics: definitions + prompts (use during or after)
These prompts help ensure we can publish credible numbers.

### Latency
- Ask for: p50 and p95 end-to-end latency (client → Redwood → client) and/or “model time” if available.
- Prompts:
  - “What is the typical prompt length and output length for these measurements?”
  - “Are you measuring streaming time-to-first-token (TTFT) or full completion time?”
  - “What region was the traffic served from?”

### Throughput
- Ask for: requests/sec, concurrent requests, tokens/sec, peak hour stats.
- Prompts:
  - “What does peak look like? How often do you hit it?”
  - “Any burst events you designed for?”

### Reliability
- Ask for: error rate, timeout rate, disconnects, availability, incident count/MTTR (if they track it).
- Prompts:
  - “What are your most common error classes and how did they change?”
  - “What was the biggest reliability win?”

### Cost
- Ask for: cost per 1k tokens, cost per query, infra cost per month, or blended unit cost.
- Prompts:
  - “Does cost include compute only, or also engineering time/ops overhead?”
  - “Did caching/batching/quantization change cost? By how much?”

### Quality / output correctness
- Ask for: eval harness results, acceptance rate, deflection metrics, human ratings.
- Prompts:
  - “How do you detect regressions when changing model versions?”
  - “What quality threshold must be met before rollout?”

## Security & compliance question set (use selectively; keep it publish-safe)
Use this for regulated customers and Private deployments.

1. Data classification: what data types are in prompts/outputs (PII/PHI/PCI)?
2. Retention: do you require zero retention or fixed retention windows?
3. Audit logs: what events/fields are required (request metadata, admin actions)?
4. Key management: do you require customer-managed keys? Any HSM requirements?
5. Network controls: VPC peering, private endpoints, egress restrictions
6. Compliance: which frameworks matter (SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, etc.)?
7. Approvals: who must review public language (security, legal, comms)?

**Publishing rule of thumb:**
- OK to publish: “customer-managed keys via cloud KMS,” “VPC deployment,” “audit logs enabled,” “data residency requirement met.”
- Avoid publishing: exact network topology, internal CIDRs, detailed security tooling list, retention specifics that reveal internal policies, named regulators/auditors.

## Follow-up: what to request after the interview
Send a short list, not a big form.

- Confirm spokesperson name/title and preferred company description
- Written confirmation of:
  - key metrics (values + window + baseline)
  - what can be public vs internal-only
- Optional assets:
  - architecture diagram sketch (we can redraw)
  - anonymized screenshots of dashboards
  - approved customer logo file (if public)

## Red flags (escalate early)
Escalate to PMM + Legal + Security/Claims review (Naomi Feldman) if:
- The customer wants to publish claims that imply guarantees beyond current SLAs
- Metrics are not reproducible or source is unclear (“we feel it’s faster”)
- The story requires disclosing sensitive deployment/security details
- The customer asks to mention competitor names or comparative claims without proof

## Timeboxing guide (cheat sheet)
- If the customer is talkative: prioritize **baseline → decision → architecture → outcomes**.
- If time is short: skip tool details and go straight to **metrics + constraints + decision rationale**.

## Reference-call-only mini-script (15 minutes)
Use when building an internal reference profile.
1) Use case + who uses it (3 min)
2) Deployment mode + why (3 min)
3) Top 2 measurable outcomes (5 min)
4) Topics they will discuss / avoid (2 min)
5) Scheduling windows + preferred contact (2 min)

## Appendix A: Example “measurement notes” wording (publishable)
Use these patterns to keep numbers honest.
- “Measured over a 30-day production window during peak business hours; p95 end-to-end latency.”
- “Baseline from prior vendor measured on the same prompt distribution and region.”
- “Cost per query calculated as (token cost + platform fees) divided by completed requests; excludes internal engineering time.”

## Appendix B: Safe architecture detail checklist (what we can usually include)
- Workload type (RAG search, support agent, summarization)
- Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
- High-level components (API gateway, app server, vector DB, Redwood)
- Non-sensitive controls (rate limits, caching, fallbacks, canary rollouts)
- Observability primitives (dashboards, tracing, alerts) without vendor-sensitive specifics

## Appendix C: Closing script
“Thanks—this was extremely helpful. Next steps: we’ll draft a narrative and propose a small set of publishable metrics and quotes. You’ll receive the draft for review, and we won’t publish anything until you approve it in writing. We’ll also confirm the reference-call process and boundaries based on what you’re comfortable discussing.”
